# The Heat Is Unequal: How Cities Can Survive a Hotter Summer

Every summer, cities become measurably hotter than the countryside around them. This phenomenon, the urban heat island effect, occurs because asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, while the scarcity of vegetation eliminates the natural cooling that evaporation provides. The temperature difference between a city and its rural surroundings can reach several degrees Fahrenheit during the day and as much as twenty degrees at night. As climate change pushes heat waves to become longer, more frequent, and more intense, this gap is no longer a curiosity of urban meteorology—it is a matter of life and death. Heat already kills more Americans in a typical year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and those deaths are concentrated in cities. The good news is that cities have real tools to make summer heat bearable. The challenge is that these tools require money, space, and political will, and they involve genuine tradeoffs that residents must weigh.
